To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
SPARC is a potent inhibitor of endothelial cell proliferation and migration, and that it is an endogenous angiogenesis inhibitor in vivo.
SPARC inhibits endothelial cell proliferation by interfering with bFGF signaling and that this effect is dependent on the presence of a functional heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) core.
SPARC is a negative regulator of vascular morphogenesis and that its effects on endothelial cell behavior are mediated through the cell cycle and cell-matrix adhesion pathways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of SPARC as a modulator of vascular morphogenesis.
the molecular mechanisms that control angiogenesis and the role of matricellular proteins in this process.
the regulation of endothelial cell behavior in the context of angiogenesis and vasculogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SPARC is a negative regulator of vascular morphogenesis, which can be modulated by the local microenvironment.
SPARC is a negative regulator of angiogenesis and that this activity is mediated by its ability to bind to the extracellular matrix.
SPARC is a negative modulator of angiogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SPARC is a multifunctional matricellular protein that modulates angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo by interacting with the extracellular matrix, cell adhesion receptors, and growth factors.
SPARC is an angiogenesis inhibitor that can also function as a positive regulator of angiogenesis.

the matricellular proteins, including SPARC, are involved in the control of angiogenesis and vascular morphogenesis by regulating the balance between cell-matrix interactions and growth factors that signal through specific receptors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SPARC is a key regulator of the angiogenic switch.
